questions.text: For the named filler, determine its exact clinical scope in small-cell lung carcinoma; use pathology evidence for morphology, distinguish generic from malignant pleural effusion, and treat the AJCC-v7 Stage IIIB versus M1a/stage-IV fact as context while answering the intended clinical scope neutrally.

claims.source_fact: SCLC is a poorly differentiated high-grade neuroendocrine carcinoma, but some tumors lack standard neuroendocrine markers.
The review describes SCLC as poorly differentiated and high grade.
A minority of SCLC is negative for all standard neuroendocrine markers.
AJCC v7 assigns malignant pleural effusion to M1a/stage IV; generic pleural effusion alone does not establish malignancy.
SCLC is described as a high-grade carcinoma.
Extensive intratumoral necrosis is often recognized, which does not mean universal.
SCLC is neuroendocrine, while a minority lacks all standard neuroendocrine markers.
Peripheral palisading is listed as one possible SCLC growth feature.
Nuclear molding is described as well developed in tightly cohesive sheets.
The review reports a usually very high mitotic rate of 10 mitoses per 10 high-power fields.
The review's entity is small cell lung carcinoma and provides its histopathologic features.
The reviewed entity is a carcinoma arising in the lung.
Most SCLC tumors are hilar or perihilar and spread along bronchial submucosa; this does not prove a universal bronchus subsite.
The controlling historical source is the AJCC seventh-edition lung staging table.
AJCC v7 requires M0 for stage IIIB, while malignant pleural effusion is M1a.
AJCC v7 places malignant pleural effusion in stage IV; it does not define the separate VALG extensive-stage concept.
SCLC is one subtype of lung carcinoma; the broad parent does not express stage intent.
Pathology evidence identifies SCLC but does not by itself establish the separate extensive-stage morphology concept.
